evidence: Cic. Tusc. 1.7–8: scholās Graecōrum mōre habēre
terms.comment: Greek σχολή, leisure and what scholars do with it: a lecture or a learned discussion, and then the place where it is given, a school (Lewis & Short). To give a lecture is scholam habēre; to attend a teacher’s lectures, simply audīre (tē, Marce fīlī, annum jam audientem Cratippum, Cic. Off. 1.1).

evidence: Cic. Att. 15.17.2: vel in acroāsī audeam legere
terms.comment: Greek ἀκρόασις, a hearing: a lecture or reading before an audience. To give one, acroāsin facere (Suet. Gram. 2; Traupman 339).

terms.gloss: a reading of a text aloud, with explanation
terms.comment: The teacher reads a text aloud and explains it (see read aloud, praelegere); Lewis & Short: post-Augustan.

phrases.latin: ut jam etiam scholās Graecōrum mōre habēre audērēmus … itaque diērum quīnque scholās, ut Graecī appellant, in totidem librōs contulī
phrases.english: so that I even dared to give lectures in the Greek manner … so I have gathered the five days’ lectures, as the Greeks call them, into as many books

phrases.latin: ipsīus litterae sīc et φιλοστόργως et εὐπινῶς scrīptae ut eās vel in acroāsī audeam legere
phrases.english: his own letters are written so affectionately and so elegantly that I would dare to read them out even at a public lecture

acroasis.html: Greek ἀκρόασις, from ἀκροάομαι, with the short ἀ of ἄκρος; Lewis & Short marks the same a short in acrochordon, acropodium, acrōtēria, also from ἄκρος.
